Enos
ē'nos
n. (the son of Seth and grandson of Adam, in whose days men began to call upon the name of the LORD; written Enosh in the Chronicles)
From Hebrew 'Enosh, man — and specifically man in his frailty and mortality, from a root meaning to be weak or incurable, as distinguished from 'adam, man from the ground, and 'ish, man as male. Luke gives the Greek form Enos in the genealogy of our Lord.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Enos is the third man in the line of promise, and his birth carries one of the most weighted notices in Genesis: “And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD” (Gen 4:26). The verse stands at the end of the chapter that has just traced the line of Cain through city-building, polygamy and Lamech's boast of murder. Against that, one sentence: men began to call upon the name of the LORD. Whether the phrase marks the beginning of public, corporate worship or the beginning of men being called by the name of the LORD, the point is the same — in the generation of the man whose name means frail mortal, the true religion appears in the earth as a visible thing. His life is then given in the register: “And Enos lived ninety years, and begat Cainan” (Gen 5:9), and “And all the days of Enos were nine hundred and five years: and he died” (Gen 5:11). Luke sets him in the descent of Christ: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God” (Luk 3:38). Nine hundred and five years, one recorded sentence about his generation, and a place in the line that ends at Bethlehem.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Enos; in sacred history he is the son of Seth, in whose days men began to call upon the name of the LORD.

expand to see more

ENOS, n. Man, mortal man; the son of Seth and grandson of Adam.

In the Chronicles the name is written Enosh, and in Luke, in the Greek form, Enos.

In his days men began to call upon the name of the LORD.

He lived ninety years and begat Cainan, and all his days were nine hundred and five years.

He stands third in the genealogy of our Saviour as it is reckoned by Luke.

Key Scripture

Gen 4:26 — "And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD."

Gen 5:9 — "And Enos lived ninety years, and begat Cainan:"

Gen 5:11 — "And all the days of Enos were nine hundred and five years: and he died."

Luk 3:38 — "Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God."

Modern Corruption

The rise of religion in Genesis 4:26 is commonly explained as the natural evolution of primitive man's response to nature. Scripture presents worship as the response of a people to a God who has already spoken and already promised a Seed.

expand to see more

The standard account of religion's origin runs from animism through polytheism to monotheism, with Israel's faith a late refinement of a long human development. Genesis reverses the sequence completely. God walks with man in the garden; man falls; God gives the promise of the Seed and clothes the guilty with skins, which required a death; Abel brings a firstling of his flock and is accepted, Cain brings the fruit of the ground and is not; and then, in the days of Enos, calling on the name of the LORD becomes a public practice. Worship in Scripture is never man's upward guess. It is the response of sinners to a revelation and a promise already given.

The name matters to the point. Enosh is man as feeble, mortal, incurable — the word the Psalms use when they ask, “What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?” (Psa 8:4). It was in the generation of frail man that men began to call upon the LORD, and that order is the gospel in miniature: the creature calls because he knows what he is and knows Who has spoken. Paul quotes the promise that runs from this point to the end: “whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom 10:13).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Enosh (H583), Enos; 'enosh (H582), man, mortal, frail; qara' beshem YHWH (H7121 with H8034), to call upon the name of the LORD; Sheth (H8352), Seth; Greek Enōs (G1800).

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Enosh (H583) — Enos; the son of Seth.

Hebrew 'enosh (H582) — man in his frailty and mortality.

Hebrew qara' (H7121) — to call, to call upon; the verb of Genesis 4:26.

Hebrew Sheth (H8352) — Seth; the appointed seed in place of Abel.

Greek Enōs (G1800) — Enos; the form Luke uses in the descent of Christ.

Usage

"“Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD” — public worship appearing in the earth."

"“And all the days of Enos were nine hundred and five years: and he died” — the refrain of the chapter."

"“Which was the son of Enos” — a link in the genealogy of the Lord."
